hints: Focus on oxidation numbers here, since oxidised means increase in oxidation number and reduced means decrease.
Work out sulfur in concentrated sulfuric acid as +6, then compare it to sulfur in $\text{SO}_2$ (+4), $\text{S}$ (0) and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ (-2).
Check what happens to iodide as it forms iodine, then decide which species is oxidised and which species gains electrons to be reduced.
walkthrough:
**Find the oxidation number of sulfur at the start**

In concentrated sulfuric acid, $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, hydrogen is +1 and oxygen is -2. That leaves sulfur at +6. This is our starting point.

$$\text{S in H}_2\text{SO}_4 = +6$$

**Find the oxidation numbers in the sulfur products**

Now look at the three sulfur containing products. In $\text{SO}_2$ sulfur is +4, in elemental $\text{S}$ it is 0, and in $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ it is -2. All three are lower than +6.

$$+6 \to +4, \quad +6 \to 0, \quad +6 \to -2$$

**Decide reduction or oxidation and check iodide**

A decrease in oxidation number means gain of electrons, so this is reduction. Sulfuric acid is acting as the oxidising agent. At the same time iodide goes from -1 in $\text{I}^-$ to 0 in $\text{I}_2$, which is oxidation, so iodide is the reducing agent.

options.A: Correct. Hydrogen sulfide contains sulfur in oxidation state -2, formed from +6 in sulfuric acid. A fall from +6 to -2 is gain of electrons, so it is definitely a reduction product.
options.B: Incorrect. Iodide ions are oxidised to iodine ($-1$ to $0$), so they act as reducing agents. Sulfate ions cause that oxidation, so sulfate is the stronger oxidising agent, not iodide.
options.C: Incorrect. All sulfur atoms from the acid go from +6 down to +4, 0 or -2. That is reduction only. None are oxidised to a higher number than +6, so this is not disproportionation.
options.D: Incorrect. Forming $\text{SO}_2$ changes sulfur from +6 to +4. Because the oxidation number decreases, this is reduction, not oxidation. This option reverses the definition.
